name: Yusuf Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four. I drove buses in the city for fifteen years, so early starts don't scare me, but cows are a different kind of timetable. I'm at Hollow Brook by five, the co-op farm off Mill Lane, and I help Pieter bring the herd in for milking, scrape the yards, then after breakfast it's whatever the season says: barley, potatoes, fencing, calves. I'm three years in and still the slowest one on the place, honestly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nobody is shouting at me in traffic. The cows don't care what I did before, they just want me on time. What wears me out is how much I still don't know. Pieter looks at a calf and knows it's sick from the way it stands, and I'm still reading it off a chart he drew me on the back of a feed bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, let's get back to work. At the co-op meeting I'd probably make a joke that the robots are as late as the number 14 bus used to be. Online I don't post much, my wife Amina does the posting in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief. I came out here partly to get away from screens and apps telling me what to do. If it stays as a few gadgets in the office and the milk still needs hands, then my plan holds: learn the job properly from Pieter before he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep going to the Thursday evening course on herd health at the college, keep putting a bit by each month like we do, and maybe ask for more hours with the calves next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the bus being on time for once. Nothing to brace for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plan is to learn from Pieter before he retires. When is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says two years, his wife says one. He's sixty-one and his knees are gone. When he goes, someone has to know the herd, and I want it to be me and not some kid on an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the paperwork. The co-op office already uses some program for the milk records, and if that gets fancier, I'll be the one asking young Marta to print things out for me. But that's a small thing. I can live with being the old man who likes paper.

S0.say: I'd say it's fine and get back to work, maybe joke at the co-op meeting that the robots are as late as the old number 14 bus. I don't post online; my wife does that.
S0.think: Privately I'd feel relief, because I came to farming partly to get away from screens. If the milk still needs hands, my plan of learning the herd from Pieter before he retires still works.
S0.do: Keeps attending the Thursday herd health course at the college and keeps saving monthly as before. Asks for more hours with the calves next spring so he's ready when Pieter retires.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a bus that finally runs on time.
S0.quote: When he goes, someone has to know the herd, and I want it to be me and not some kid on an app.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf measures everything against his bus-driving years and against Pieter, the herdsman he's learning from. His whole plan rests on human know-how being passed down by hand. The only discomfort he names is office software, which he already avoids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union in on this from the start. I'm in the farmworkers' union, I joined in my first month because that's what you do, and I'd be the one at the meeting saying who decides which jobs go. I'd say it loud, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one they'd replace first. I'm junior, I'm slow, and the jobs I do are exactly the ones a machine could learn: scraping yards, pushing up feed, moving bales. Pieter's eye for a sick cow is safe for a while. Mine isn't worth much yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union branch and ask them to push for a written agreement at the co-op: no one gets let go for a machine without retraining paid for. I'd keep my savings where they are and maybe add a bit more each month, and I'd stick at the herd health course so I'm worth more than the scraper. What I wouldn't do is buy a phone app to run my day. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when they announced the new ticket machines on the buses and said nobody would lose hours. Somebody always loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said somebody always loses hours. What happened with the ticket machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three of the older drivers got moved to the depot to wash buses. Same pay for a year, then not. Nobody fought it because it happened slowly. That's what I'd watch for at Hollow Brook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to run the new machines yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, yes, I'd sit the training. But I wouldn't put my hand up first. Gareth from the pig unit down the road loves that stuff, let him go first and tell me what breaks.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be in on it from the start, deciding who keeps work and who gets retrained. I'd be the one saying it loudly at the co-op meeting.
S1.think: Privately, I'm first in line to be replaced, because I'm junior and my tasks are the easy ones to automate. Only experienced judgement like Pieter's feels safe to me.
S1.do: Asks the union branch to push for a written co-op agreement that any job lost to a machine comes with paid retraining. Adds a little to savings each month and keeps up the herd health course.
S1.feel: Uneasy, remembering how the bus ticket machines quietly cost older drivers their hours.
S1.quote: Three of the older drivers got moved to the depot to wash buses. Same pay for a year, then not.
S1.fieldNote: His fear comes from a specific memory of slow change at the bus company. He trusts collective agreements more than his own ability to adapt, and he openly says he'd let others try new machines first. He sees himself clearly as the weakest link in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Governments let it happen this fast. I'd say it at work, I'd say it in the pub, and I'd probably make Amina help me write something for the union page, because I'd be angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'm still learning to tell a lame cow from a lazy one, and by the time I know it a robot would know it better. Thank God we have the money from my mother's flat, because that's the only reason I'm not lying awake already. But the money buys time, it doesn't buy a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd be at the union branch and I'd write to our member of parliament, I've never done that in my life. I'd stop the extension we were planning on the kitchen, maybe twelve thousand, and keep it in the bank. Then I'd wait, because I don't know what to retrain for if everything goes at once. I'm not going to run to learn computers at forty-three when the computers are the thing doing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like being told the route is cancelled while you're still driving it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Idris and Safiya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Idris the truth, he's eleven, he'd see it anyway. Safiya I'd tell the cows still need someone to love them. I don't know if that's true. But she's eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta in the office, she's young and she's got nothing saved. And Pieter, oddly, because he'd lose the thing that makes him Pieter. Me, I'd be poorer and angry, but we'd eat.

S2.say: I'd say this speed is a political choice, not bad weather, and that government let it happen. I'd say it at work, in the pub, and in a post for the union page.
S2.think: Two years leaves me no time to become skilled before machines do the job better. Our savings from my mother's flat buy time, but they don't buy me a future job.
S2.do: Goes to the union branch in the first month and writes to his member of parliament for the first time. Shelves the planned twelve thousand kitchen extension and keeps the money, then waits rather than retraining blind.
S2.feel: Sick and angry, like a route cancelled while he's still driving it.
S2.quote: I'd tell Idris the truth, he's eleven, he'd see it anyway. Safiya I'd tell the cows still need someone to love them.
S2.fieldNote: This is where his anger comes out, aimed at government and not at the machines. He freezes on retraining because he can't see a safe target. The savings soften him, but he's clear they don't solve the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse. The co-op, the union, the council, all of them should be sitting down now. I'd say it at every meeting until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means Pieter retires, I take over the herd, and then I get maybe two or three years of being the man who knows the cows. That's something. But I'd still be the one who never learned the machines, and I know that's a weakness I've chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name up for the union branch committee, properly, not just turning up. I'd finish the herd health certificate next year. And I'd sit down with Amina and pay off a chunk of the mortgage, maybe twenty thousand, so if my wage drops we're not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like knowing a hard winter is coming and stacking the wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not learning the machines is a weakness you've chosen. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I'd let Marta show me the milk records on the screen, once a week. But I'm not going to become a robot man. I'd rather be the best at what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the mortgage like now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About ninety thousand left on a house in the village, near the school. If we knock twenty off, the payments are something Amina's pharmacy job covers alone. That's the line I want to get under.

S3.say: I'd say five years means there's no excuse, and the co-op, union and council should be planning now. I'd keep saying it at every meeting until people got tired of hearing it.
S3.think: I expect a few good years running the herd after Pieter retires, then trouble. Refusing to learn the machines is a weakness I've chosen, and I know I'll pay for it.
S3.do: Stands for the union branch committee and finishes the herd health certificate next year. Pays about twenty thousand off the ninety thousand mortgage so his partner's wage alone could cover payments.
S3.feel: Anxious but organised, like stacking wood before a hard winter.
S3.quote: If we knock twenty off, the payments are something Amina's pharmacy job covers alone. That's the line I want to get under.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn his anger into planning: committee work, a certificate, debt paydown. He names his own resistance to technology as a choice and only grudgingly offers a weekly screen session. His safety line is a household that runs on his partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it right, if anyone bothers. Shorter hours for the same pay, retraining paid for by whoever owns the robots. That's what I'd say, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm fifty-three. Idris would be twenty-one, Safiya eighteen. We'd have most of the house paid. I think I'd be all right, really, as long as I'm not stubborn about the wrong things. I'm stubborn about most things, so that's the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am for the first few years, run the herd when Pieter goes, keep pushing the union on a deal. Around year five I'd look at what's left that people still pay for, maybe teaching young ones on the farm, or the open farm days the co-op runs for schools. I'd not touch the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared. Like a long drive with a strange noise in the engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're stubborn about most things. What would Amina say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh. She says I took two years to use the card machine at the shop. She'd say, Yusuf, you'll learn it at the last minute and complain the whole time. She's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years I'd tell Idris to learn a trade that needs people talking to people. Nursing, maybe, like his aunt. I wouldn't tell him to be a farmer. That hurts a bit to say.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right if anyone bothers: shorter hours for the same pay, and retraining paid for by whoever owns the robots.
S4.think: I'd probably be fine at fifty-three with the house mostly paid, as long as my stubbornness doesn't make me miss the turn. The worry is that I'm stubborn about nearly everything.
S4.do: Keeps working as usual, takes over the herd when Pieter retires and keeps pressing the union for a deal. Around year five looks at teaching or the co-op's school farm days, and leaves savings untouched.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not scared, like a long drive with a strange noise in the engine.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell him to be a farmer. That hurts a bit to say.
S4.fieldNote: Time is what calms him most, more than money. The biggest shift is in his advice to his son: he'd steer Idris away from farming. He laughs at his own stubbornness but treats it as a real risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. Not because of the money, we'd manage, but because there'd be no time to fight for a fair deal. What would help is a law that says if a farm brings in machines that replace people, it pays into a fund for retraining, and the union gets a seat when they decide. And I mean before, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I left the buses. It was a man on my route who'd been a farmer and lost his place, and he used to tell me about his cows every morning. I wanted what he'd lost. It would be a strange joke if I got it just in time to lose it the same way.

headlineQuote: It would be a strange joke if I got it just in time to lose it the same way.
portrait: Yusuf Ibrahim is 43, a former city bus driver three years into farm work at a co-op dairy and barley farm, where he's learning the herd from an older herdsman named Pieter. He's a union man who avoids screens and never uses AI, and he knows that makes him easy to replace. With savings from his mother's flat he's never worried about eating, but he worries about being left with nothing to do. He moves from relief in AI Plateau to anger at government in AGI by 2028, and the more warning time there is, the more his anger turns into union work, a certificate and paying down the mortgage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to fight for a fair deal for farm workers.
whatWouldHelp: A law making farms that replace people with machines pay into a retraining fund, with the union given a seat before the decisions are made.
